title: Preparing for HPC on RISC-V: Examining Vectorization and Distributed Performance of an Astrophysics Application with HPX and Kokkos
problem: Early RISC-V processors with finalized vector specifications require evaluation for HPC suitability. The challenge is porting modern C++ HPC applications to RISC-V and assessing whether variable-length vectorization and vector-chaining capabilities deliver competitive performance compared to established HPC systems.
motivation: RISC-V is gaining mainstream HPC adoption due to energy efficiency concerns, and first commercial RISC-V CPUs with vector support are now available, making viability assessment critical.
method: The researchers adapt Octo-Tiger—an astrophysics simulation built with HPX and Kokkos (C++ frameworks for parallel programming)—that models multiple physical systems in 3D with adaptive mesh refinement (uneven spatial partitioning that concentrates computation where it matters most), to run on RISC-V processors. They use std::experimental::simd, a C++ interface that exploits RISC-V's vector extension (hardware that processes multiple data values simultaneously) with variable-length vector support (adjusting to the processor's native width) and vector-chaining (efficiently linking multiple vector operations). They measure performance, scalability, and power consumption on RISC-V single board computers and directly compare the results against A64FX systems, an established Arm-based HPC processor.
key_novelty: This work provides the first thorough test of RISC-V vector processors on a real, production-grade HPC astrophysics application using HPX and Kokkos (modern C++ frameworks).
contributions: Successful port of Octo-Tiger astrophysics application to RISC-V with vector extension support
Implementation and integration of std::experimental::simd for RISC-V vectorization
Comparative performance, scalability, and power analysis against A64FX
Viability assessment of RISC-V for real-world HPC workloads
